arXiv:1203.6605v3 [math.AG] 20 Jan 2015

Polynomials with constant Hessian determinants in dimension three

Michiel de Bondt Note: The author was supported by the Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research (NWO). Affiliation: Institute for Mathematics, Astrophisics and Particle Physics Affiliation: Radboud University Nijmegen Affiliation: Email address: M.deBondt@math.ru.nl
Abstract

In this paper, we show that the Jacobian conjecture holds for gradient maps in dimension n≤3n\leq 3 over a field KK of characteristic zero. We do this by extending the following result for n≤2n\leq 2 by F. Dillen to n≤3n\leq 3: if ff is a polynomial of degree larger than two in n≤3n\leq 3 variables such that the Hessian determinant of ff is constant, then after a suitable linear transformation (replacing ff by f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) for some T∈GLn⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K)), the Hessian matrix of ff becomes zero below the anti-diagonal. The result does not hold for larger nn.

The proof of the case detℋ​f∈K∗\det{\mathcal{H}}f\in K^{*} is based on the following result, which in turn is based on the already known case detℋ​f=0\det{\mathcal{H}}f=0: if ff is a polynomial in n≤3n\leq 3 variables such that detℋ​f≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}f\neq 0, then after a suitable linear transformation, there exists a positive weight function ww on the variables such that the Hessian determinant of the ww-leading part of ff is nonzero. This result does not hold for larger nn either (even if we replace ‘positive’ by ‘nontrivial’ above).

In the last section, we show that the Jacobian conjecture holds for gradient maps over the reals whose linear part is the identity map, by proving that such gradient maps are translations (i.e. have degree 11) if they satisfy the Keller condition. We do this by showing that this problem is the polynomial case of the main result of [Pog]. For polynomials in dimension n≤3n\leq 3, we generalize this result to arbitrary fields of characteristic zero.

Key words: Hessian determinant, Jacobian conjecture, polynomial, weighted degree, anisotropic quadratic form.

2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 13F20; 14R15; 15A63.

1 Introduction

Throughout this paper, KK denotes an arbitrary field of characteristic zero. Furthermore, x1,x2,x3,…x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},\ldots are indeterminates and GLn⁡(K)\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K) is the group of invertible matrices of size n×nn\times n over KK. Applying a linear transformation on a polynomial f∈K⁡[x]=K⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]f\in K[x]=K[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}] is just replacing ff by f⁡(T​x)f(Tx), where T​xTx can be seen as a matrix product of the matrix T∈GLn⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K) and the vector x=(x1,x2,…,xn)x=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}).

Suppose that the Hessian matrix ℋ​f{\mathcal{H}}f of a polynomial f∈K⁡[x]=K⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]f\in K[x]=K[x_{1},x_{2},\allowbreak\ldots,x_{n}] is zero below the anti-diagonal. Then ℋ​f{\mathcal{H}}f can be turned into a lower triangular matrix by way of ⌊n/2⌋\lfloor n/2\rfloor row interchanges. Since the product of the diagonal entries of a lower triangular matrix is just its determinant, we can deduce that the product of the elements of the anti-diagonal of ℋ​f{\mathcal{H}}f is (−1)⌊n/2⌋​detℋ​f(-1)^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\det{\mathcal{H}}f.

But in general, the Hessian of a polynomial will not be zero below the anti-diagonal. However, if detℋ​f∈K\det{\mathcal{H}}f\in K and n≤3≤deg⁡fn\leq 3\leq\deg f, then after applying a suitable linear transformation on ff, ℋ​f{\mathcal{H}}f will indeed be zero below the anti-diagonal, where deg⁡f\deg f denotes the total degree of ff (in x1,x2,…,xnx_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}). This is our main result. As a consequence, we show that the Jacobian conjecture holds for polynomial maps over KK in dimension n≤3n\leq 3, for which the Jacobian is symmetric. Both our main result and its consequence can be found in theorem 2.1. Section 2 will be devoted to the proof of theorem 2.1.

Suppose next that detℋ​f≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}f\neq 0 for some polynomial f∈K⁡[x]=K⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]f\in K[x]=K[x_{1},x_{2},\allowbreak\ldots,x_{n}]. Now take a hyperplane SS with negative slope with respect to all coordinates of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, which intersects the newton polytope of ff only at its boundary. Let f¯\bar{f} be the part of ff consisting of the monomials whose multidegrees lie in SS. Although detℋ​f≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}f\neq 0, it is very possible that detℋ​f¯=0\det{\mathcal{H}}\bar{f}=0. However, if n≤3n\leq 3, then after applying a suitable linear transformation on ff, detℋ​f¯\det{\mathcal{H}}\bar{f} will indeed be nonzero for some hyperplane SS as above. This is our main lemma for the proof of our main result. But since it is interesting on its own, this lemma has become a theorem, namely theorem 2.2.

Example 2.3 makes clear that theorem 2.2 is no longer true in dimensions larger than three. In fact, in dimension four and up, it is possible that ff has the following property, in such a way that it cannot be undone by applying linear transformations: the property of ff that detℋ​f¯≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}\bar{f}\neq 0 is entirely encapsulated by the Newton polytope of ff. More precisely, the part of ff consisting of monomials whose supports lie on the boundary of the Newton polytope of ff is a polynomial whose Hessian determinant is zero.

The rest of this introduction will be devoted to a historical overview of the study of polynomials with constant Hessian determinants, followed by a closer look on linear transformations.

There are some very old papers devoted to the study of polynomials with constant Hessian determinants in some manner. Perhaps the oldest is an article of Paul Gordan and Max Nöther about homogeneous polynomials with Hessian determinant zero, which appeared in 1876 in [GN]. This is the most interesting case for homogeneous polynomials, because if a homogeneous polynomial h∈ℂ⁡[x]=ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]h\in{\mathbb{C}}[x]={\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}] has a constant nonzero Hessian determinant, then the Hessian matrix must be constant and nonzero, so that hh can only be a quadratic form.

For quadratic forms, basic linear algebra can be used to show that hh can be written as a polynomial in n−1n-1 (or less) linear forms over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, if and only if the Hessian determinant of hh is zero. So assume that hh is a homogeneous polynomial of degree d≥3d\geq 3. Again by basic linear algebra, it follows that hh cannot be written as a polynomial in n−1n-1 (or less) linear forms over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, in case the Hessian determinant of hh is nonzero.

But the converse may not be true. However, in [GN], the authors show that hh can indeed be written as a polynomial in n−1n-1 (or less) linear forms over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} in case n≤4n\leq 4 and hh has Hessian determinant zero, and give counterexamples for all n≥5n\geq 5 and all d≥3d\geq 3. In [dBvdE2], A. van den Essen and the author classify all (not necessarily homogeneous) polynomials h∈K⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]h\in K[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}] with n≤3n\leq 3, such that the Hessian determinant of hh is zero, where KK is a field of characteristic zero, using techniques of [GN]. We shall use these results to prove our main lemma (theorem 2.2) and the case detℋ​f=0\det{\mathcal{H}}f=0 of our main theorem (theorem 2.1).

In 1939 in [Kel], O. Keller formulated a question about constant nonzero Jacobian determinants, which is known as Keller’s problem or the Jacobian conjecture. The Jacobian conjecture asserts that FF is invertible if FF satisfies the so-called Keller condition. The Keller condition on a polynomial map FF is the property that det𝒥​F\det{\mathcal{J}}F is a nonzero constant in KK, where 𝒥​F{\mathcal{J}}F is the Jacobian matrix of FF. Since Hessians are Jacobians of gradient maps, we can ask ourselves whether the Jacobian conjecture holds for gradient maps. This was done in [vdEW], where a positive answer was given in dimension n≤4n\leq 4, for gradient maps of the form x+Hx+H with HH homogeneous. See also [dBvdE1] for this result. In [dBvdE3], A. van den Essen and the author generalized this result to dimension n≤5n\leq 5. For dimension n≤4n\leq 4, the condition that HH is homogeneous was weakened to that 𝒥​H{\mathcal{J}}H is nilpotent (the nilpotency of 𝒥​H{\mathcal{J}}H follows by way of the condition that det𝒥​F\det{\mathcal{J}}F is a nonzero constant from the homogeneity of HH).

The generalization to dimension n≤5n\leq 5 led the authors of [dBvdE3] to the discovery that the Jacobian conjecture for gradient maps is equivalent to the Jacobian conjecture, which they published in [dBvdE4], see also [dB, Cor. 1.4]. G. Meng did the same discovery, which he published as [Men, Prop. 1.4], see also [dB, Th. 1.2]. More precisely, the Jacobian conjecture in dimension nn follows from the Jacobian conjecture for gradient maps in dimension 2​n2n. Hence the Jacobian conjecture is about polynomials with constant Hessian determinants after all. We shall show that the Jacobian conjecture holds for gradient maps in dimension three. In dimension two, this problem has already been solved in 1991 by F. Dillen, see below. Notice that an affirmative answer to the same problem in dimension four would imply the planar Jacobian conjecture.

In [Men, Th. 1.3], the author proves that the Jacobian conjecture holds for real gradient maps in all dimensions, provided the linear part is equal to the identity map. We will reprove this result, by showing that real gradient maps whose linear part is the identity map are translations (i.e. have degree 11) if they satisfy the Keller condition, using results that are described below. In 1954, K. Jörgens proved in [Jör] that functions from ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2} to ℝ{\mathbb{R}} which are twice continuously differentiable and whose Hessian determinant equals one at each point are in fact quadratic polynomials. Four years later, this result was extended to ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3} and ℝ4{\mathbb{R}}^{4} by E. Calabi in [Cal], but with the extra condition that the Hessian matrix is positive definite everywhere. The polynomial

f=g⁡(x1+x3)−12​x12−12​x22+12​x32+⋯+12​xn2f=g(x_{1}+x_{3})-\tfrac{1}{2}x_{1}^{2}-\tfrac{1}{2}x_{2}^{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}x_{3}^{2}+\cdots+\tfrac{1}{2}x_{n}^{2}

shows that such an extra condition is required. An extension to arbitrary dimension was proved by A.V. Pogorelov in 1972 in [Pog], using a lemma of [Cal]. In theorem 4.2, we shall extend this result for polynomials in dimensions n≤3n\leq 3 (and for real polynomials) as follows. We shall show that a polynomial in K⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]K[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}] is a quadratic polynomial if its Hessian determinant is constant and its quadratic part does not vanish at Kn∖{0}nK^{n}\setminus\{0\}^{n}, provided n≤3n\leq 3 (or K=ℝK={\mathbb{R}}).

In 1991, F. Dillen classified all polynomials in two indeterminates over a field of characteristic zero with constant Hessian determinant in [Dil], and showed that the Jacobian conjecture holds for gradient maps in dimension two. The key point of Dillen’s classification can be seen as follows: if the degree of the polynomial is larger than two, then after a suitable linear transformation, the lower right corner of its Hessian matrix becomes zero. As mentioned above, our main result (in theorem 2.1) is a similar statement for polynomials with constant Hessian determinant in dimension three: if the degree of the polynomial is larger than two, then after a suitable linear transformation, every entry below the anti-diagonal of its Hessian matrix becomes zero. This result does not hold in dimensions larger than three and neither for quadratic polynomials over ℝ{\mathbb{R}} in dimensions two and three.

Let T∈GLn⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K). Taking the Jacobian matrix of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx), we obtain by the chain rule that

𝒥​f​(T​x)=(𝒥​f)|x=T​x⋅T{\mathcal{J}}f(Tx)=({\mathcal{J}}f)|_{x=Tx}\cdot T

where |x=g|_{x=g} stands for substituting xx by gg. Since the gradient vector, denoted by ∇\nabla, is the transpose of the Jacobian of a single polynomial, we obtain

∇f​(T​x)=Tt⋅(∇f)|x=T​x\nabla f(Tx)=T^{\rm t}\cdot(\nabla f)|_{x=Tx} (1)

where t stands for taking the transpose. Subsequently, we can take the Jacobian of (1), which is the Hessian, denoted by ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx), and again by the chain rule, we obtain

ℋ​f​(T​x)=Tt⋅(ℋ​f)|x=T​x⋅T{\mathcal{H}}f(Tx)=T^{\rm t}\cdot({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=Tx}\cdot T (2)

Formulas 1 and 2 indicate the effect of a linear transformation on the gradient and the Hessian, respectively.

Now that we know how linear transformations influence the Hessian, we are able to see that Dillen’s result cannot be extended to dimension four. Take for instance

f=(x1+x22)​x3+(x2+(x1+x22)2)​x4f=(x_{1}+x_{2}^{2})x_{3}+(x_{2}+(x_{1}+x_{2}^{2})^{2})x_{4} (3)

Then the cubic part of ff is equal to x22​x3+x12​x4x_{2}^{2}x_{3}+x_{1}^{2}x_{4}, and the rows of its Hessian, whose entries are linear forms, are independent over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. This is maintained after a linear transformation, so if we could obtain by way of a transformation that the Hessian of ff becomes zero below the anti-diagonal, the lower left corner of ℋ​f{\mathcal{H}}f would get a nontrivial linear part, because the last row of the Hessian of the cubic part of ff cannot become zero. This however contradicts that the Hessian determinant is a nonzero constant. The polynomial ff in (3) was made by applying the reduction of the Jacobian conjecture to gradient maps, as in [Men, Prop. 1.4], on the planar invertible map F=(x1+x22,x2+(x1+x22)2)F=(x_{1}+x_{2}^{2},x_{2}+(x_{1}+x_{2}^{2})^{2}).

2 Results and proof of main result

First, we formulate our main result. At the end of this section, we will derive the main result from other results in this section.

Theorem 2.1 (Main result).

Let KK be a field of characteristic zero and f∈K⁡[x]=K⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]f\in K[x]=K[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}] be a polynomial of degree dd. If n≤3n\leq 3, then ∇f\nabla f satisfies the Jacobian conjecture.

If n≤3≤dn\leq 3\leq d and detℋ​f∈K\det{\mathcal{H}}f\in K, then there exists a T∈GLn⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K) such that all entries below the anti-diagonal of the Hessian of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) are zero. In particular, the quadratic part of ff vanishes somewhere at Kn∖{0}nK^{n}\setminus\{0\}^{n} when 2≤n≤32\leq n\leq 3, namely at the last column of TT.

The condition d≥3d\geq 3 for the existence of TT as claimed in theorem 2.1 is necessary (except for algebraically closed fields KK). Take for instance f=12​x12+12​x22+⋯+12​xn2f=\frac{1}{2}x_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x_{2}^{2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{2}x_{n}^{2}. Then ff has no nontrivial zero over ℝ{\mathbb{R}}, so ff does not vanish at the last column of any T∈GLn⁡(ℝ)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}({\mathbb{R}}). See section 4 for more results about the real numbers.

Let KK be a field. We call w:K⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]→ℝ∪{−∞}w:K[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}]\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}\cup\{-\infty\} a weight function if w⁡(0)=−∞w(0)=-\infty,

w(x1α1x2α2⋯xnαn)=α1w(x1)+α2w(x2)+⋯+αnw(xn)∈ℝw(x_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}x_{2}^{\alpha_{2}}\cdots x_{n}^{\alpha_{n}})=\alpha_{1}w(x_{1})+\alpha_{2}w(x_{2})+\cdots+\alpha_{n}w(x_{n})\in{\mathbb{R}}

and, in case g≠0g\neq 0,

w⁡(g)=max⁡{w⁡(t)∣t is a term of g (with nonzero coefficient)}w(g)=\max\{w(t)\mid\mbox{$t$ is a term of $g$ (with nonzero coefficient)}\}

The ww-leading part of a polynomial gg is the sum of the monomials ct​tc_{t}t of gg (with nonzero coefficient ctc_{t}), for which w⁡(t)=w⁡(g)w(t)=w(g).

In order to prove our main theorem, we use the following theorem, which we prove in section 3.

Theorem 2.2.

Let KK be a field of characteristic zero and assume that f∈K⁡[x]=K⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]f\in K[x]=K[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}] satisfies detℋ​f≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}f\neq 0. If n≤3n\leq 3, then there exist a T∈GLn⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K) and a weight function 0<w⁡(x1)≤w⁡(x2)≤⋯≤w⁡(xn)0<w(x_{1})\leq w(x_{2})\leq\cdots\leq w(x_{n}), such that the Hessian determinant of the ww-leading part of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) is nonzero.

The example below shows that the above theorem cannot be extended to dimensions larger than three.

Example 2.3.

Let n≥4n\geq 4 and

f:=x1​x2+t​x1​x22+(x2+x1​x3)3+x14​(1+x4)+(x57+⋯+xnn+2)f:=x_{1}x_{2}+tx_{1}x_{2}^{2}+(x_{2}+x_{1}x_{3})^{3}+x_{1}^{4}(1+x_{4})+(x_{5}^{7}+\cdots+x_{n}^{n+2})

Then detℋ​f=t​g\det{\mathcal{H}}f=tg, where

g=−1450(n+1)!(n+2)!x19(x2+x1x3)x55⋯xnn∈ℤ[x]∖{0}g=-\tfrac{1}{450}(n+1)!\,(n+2)!\,x_{1}^{9}(x_{2}+x_{1}x_{3})x_{5}^{5}\cdots x_{n}^{n}\in{\mathbb{Z}}[x]\setminus\{0\}

In particular,

detℋ⁡(f|t=0)=0≠g=detℋ⁡(f|t=1)\det{\mathcal{H}}(f|_{t=0})=0\neq g=\det{\mathcal{H}}(f|_{t=1})

Consequently, for each T∈GLn⁡(ℂ)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) and each (w⁡(x1),w⁡(x2),…,w⁡(xn))∈ℝn∖{0}n(w(x_{1}),w(x_{2}),\ldots,w(x_{n}))\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}\setminus\{0\}^{n}, the ww-leading part of f⁡(T​x)|t=0f(Tx)|_{t=0} has Hessian determinant zero. We will show in section 3 that the same holds for f⁡(T​x)|t=1f(Tx)|_{t=1}, although its Hessian determinant is nonzero. Hence the condition n≤3n\leq 3 in theorem 2.2 is necessary.

This example was inspired by formula (9) in [dBvdE2, Th. 3.5], and f|t=0f|_{t=0} is of the form of this formula in dimension n=4n=4.

As announced, we will use results of [dBvdE2] in our proof. These results are used in the proof of theorem 2.2, and are as follows.

Theorem 2.4.

Let KK be a field of characteristic zero. Suppose that h∈K⁡[x]=K⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]h\in K[x]=K[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}] has no terms of degree less than two and that detℋ​h=0\det{\mathcal{H}}h=0. If n≤3n\leq 3, then there exists a T∈GLn⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K) such that all entries below the anti-diagonal of the Hessian of h⁡(T​x)h(Tx) are zero.

  1. i)

    If n=2n=2, then h∈K⁡[l1]h\in K[l_{1}] for some linear form l1∈K⁡[x]l_{1}\in K[x].

  2. ii)

    If n=3n=3, then either h∈K⁡[l1,l2]h\in K[l_{1},l_{2}] for some linear forms l1,l2∈K⁡[x]l_{1},l_{2}\in K[x], or h=g1​(l1)​x1+g2​(l1)​x2+g3​(l1)​x3h=g_{1}(l_{1})x_{1}+g_{2}(l_{1})x_{2}+g_{3}(l_{1})x_{3} for some linear form l1∈K⁡[x]l_{1}\in K[x] and polynomials g1,g2,g3∈K⁡[x1]g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}\in K[x_{1}]. Furthermore, the leading homogeneous part of hh is of the form l1deg⁡h−1​l4l_{1}^{\deg h-1}l_{4} for some linear form l4∈K⁡[x]l_{4}\in K[x] in the latter case.

Proof.

Since the claims of theorem 2.4 are void when n=1n=1, the cases n=2n=2 and n=3n=3 remain. Write l=(l1,l2,…,ln)l=(l_{1},l_{2},\ldots,l_{n}).

  1. i)

    Assume that n=2n=2. [dBvdE2, Th. 3.1] tells us that there exists a T∈GLn⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K) such that h⁡(T​x)∈K⁡[x1]h(Tx)\in K[x_{1}]. Hence TT is as claimed and we can take l=T−1​xl=T^{-1}x to get h∈K⁡[l1]h\in K[l_{1}].

  2. ii)

    Assume that n=3n=3. [dBvdE2, Th. 3.3] tells us that there exists a T∈GLn⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K) such that h⁡(T​x)∈K⁡[x1,x2]h(Tx)\in K[x_{1},x_{2}] or h⁡(T​x)h(Tx) is of the form a1​(x1)+a2​(x1)​x2+a2​(x3)​x3a_{1}(x_{1})+a_{2}(x_{1})x_{2}+a_{2}(x_{3})x_{3} for polynomials a1,a2,a3a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}. Again, TT is as claimed and we can take l=T−1​xl=T^{-1}x. Then h=a1​(l1)+a2​(l1)​l2+a3​(l1)​l3h=a_{1}(l_{1})+a_{2}(l_{1})l_{2}+a_{3}(l_{1})l_{3} in case h∉K⁡[l1,l2]h\notin K[l_{1},l_{2}], which we assume from now on.

    Since hh, a2​(l1)​l2a_{2}(l_{1})l_{2} and a3​(l1)​l3a_{3}(l_{1})l_{3} have no constant terms, neither has a1​(l1)a_{1}(l_{1}), and we see that l1|a1​(l1)l_{1}\mid a_{1}(l_{1}). Consequently, h=b1​(l1)​l1+b2​(l1)​l2+b3​(l1)​l3h=b_{1}(l_{1})l_{1}+b_{2}(l_{1})l_{2}+b_{3}(l_{1})l_{3} for polynomials b1,b2,b3b_{1},b_{2},b_{3}. But each of the linear forms l1,l2,l3l_{1},l_{2},l_{3} is a linear combination of x1,x2,x3x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}, whence h=g1​(l1)​x1+g2​(l1)​x2+g3​(l1)​x3h=g_{1}(l_{1})x_{1}+g_{2}(l_{1})x_{2}+g_{3}(l_{1})x_{3} for polynomials g1,g2,g3g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}.

    If c1,c2,c3c_{1},c_{2},c_{3} are the coefficients of degree deg⁡h−1\deg h-1 of g1,g2,g3g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}, respectively, then the leading homogeneous part of hh is equal to l1deg⁡h−1​(c1​x1+c2​x2+c3​x3)l_{1}^{\deg h-1}(c_{1}x_{1}+c_{2}x_{2}+c_{3}x_{3}), which is as claimed with l4=c1​x1+c2​x2+c3​x3l_{4}=c_{1}x_{1}+c_{2}x_{2}+c_{3}x_{3}. ∎

Proof of theorem 2.1.

There is nothing to be proved when detℋ​f∉K\det{\mathcal{H}}f\notin K, so let detℋ​f∈K\det{\mathcal{H}}f\in K. Notice that the Jacobian conjecture is trivially satisfied when n=1n=1 or d≤2d\leq 2. Since there is nothing additionally to be proved in both cases, we may assume that 2≤n≤3≤d2\leq n\leq 3\leq d.

  1. i)

    We first show that a TT as given exists. If detℋ​f=0\det{\mathcal{H}}f=0, then the existence of TT follows from theorem 2.4. Hence suppose that detℋ​f∈K∗\det{\mathcal{H}}f\in K^{*}. By theorem 2.2, there exist a T∈GLn⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K) and a weight function 0<w⁡(x1)≤w⁡(x2)≤⋯≤w⁡(xn)0<w(x_{1})\leq w(x_{2})\leq\cdots\leq w(x_{n}) such that the Hessian determinant of the ww-leading part of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) is nonzero. Since detℋ​f∈K∗\det{\mathcal{H}}f\in K^{*}, the Hessian determinant of the ww-leading part of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) is a nonzero constant as well. On the other hand, all terms of this determinant have weight nw(f(Tx))−2w(x1x2⋯xn)nw(f(Tx))-2w(x_{1}x_{2}\cdots x_{n}), so

    nw(f(Tx))−2w(x1x2⋯xn)=0nw(f(Tx))-2w(x_{1}x_{2}\cdots x_{n})=0 (4)

    By d≥3d\geq 3, we have (ℋ​f​(T​x))i​j∉K({\mathcal{H}}f(Tx))_{ij}\notin K for some i,ji,j. On account of 0<w⁡(x1)≤w⁡(x2)≤⋯≤w⁡(xn)0<w(x_{1})\leq w(x_{2})\leq\cdots\leq w(x_{n}) and (4), we have

    w⁡((ℋ​f​(T​x))n​nn−1​(ℋ​f​(T​x))i​j)≤n​w​(f⁡(T​x))−w⁡(xi​xj​xnn−1​xnn−1)≤0w\big(({\mathcal{H}}f(Tx))_{nn}^{n-1}({\mathcal{H}}f(Tx))_{ij}\big)\leq nw(f(Tx))-w(x_{i}x_{j}x_{n}^{n-1}x_{n}^{n-1})\leq 0

    so (ℋ​f​(T​x))n​nn−1=0({\mathcal{H}}f(Tx))_{nn}^{n-1}=0 and TT is as claimed when n=2n=2. If n=3n=3, then we have

    w⁡((ℋ​f​(T​x))32n−1​(ℋ​f​(T​x))i​j)≤n​w​(f⁡(T​x))−w⁡(xi​xj​x2n−1​x3n−1)≤0w\big(({\mathcal{H}}f(Tx))_{32}^{n-1}({\mathcal{H}}f(Tx))_{ij}\big)\leq nw(f(Tx))-w(x_{i}x_{j}x_{2}^{n-1}x_{3}^{n-1})\leq 0

    so (ℋ​f​(T​x))32n−1=0({\mathcal{H}}f(Tx))_{32}^{n-1}=0 as well and TT is as claimed when n=3n=3, too.

  2. ii)

    We next show that the quadratic part of ff vanishes on the last column T​enTe_{n} of TT. On account of n≥2n\geq 2, the lower right corner entry of ℋ​f​(T​x){\mathcal{H}}f(Tx) vanishes. Hence f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) has no term which is divisible by xn2x_{n}^{2}. So every quadratic term of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) vanishes at the nn-th standard basis unit vector ene_{n}, and the quadratic part of ff vanishes at the last column T​enTe_{n} of TT.

  3. iii)

    At last, we show that ∇f\nabla f satisfies the Jacobian conjecture. So assume that detℋ​f∈K∗\det{\mathcal{H}}f\in K^{*}. By (1) and detTt=detT≠0\det T^{\rm t}=\det T\neq 0, it suffices to show that F:=∇f​(T​x)F:=\nabla f(Tx) is invertible. Since ℋ⁡(f⁡(T​x))=𝒥​F{\mathcal{H}}(f(Tx))={\mathcal{J}}F, the invertibility of FF follows from lemma 2.5 below. ∎

Lemma 2.5.

Suppose that AA is a commutative ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-algebra and F∈A​[x]n=A​[x1,x2,…,xn]nF\in A[x]^{n}=A[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}]^{n}. If all entries below the anti-diagonal of 𝒥​F{\mathcal{J}}F are zero and det𝒥​F∈A∗\det{\mathcal{J}}F\in A^{*}, then FF is invertible.

Proof.

Since the entries below the anti-diagonal of 𝒥​F{\mathcal{J}}F are zero, we see that Fn+1−i∈A⁡[x1,x2,…,xi]F_{n+1-i}\in A[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{i}] for each ii. Hence it follows from det𝒥​F∈A∗\det{\mathcal{J}}F\in A^{*}, that the entries on the anti-diagonal of 𝒥​F{\mathcal{J}}F are nonzero constants. Say that these constants are c1,c2,…,cnc_{1},c_{2},\ldots,\allowbreak c_{n} from left to right. Then Fn−c1​x1∈AF_{n}-c_{1}x_{1}\in A and Fn+1−i−ci​xi∈A⁡[x1,x2,…,xi−1]F_{n+1-i}-c_{i}x_{i}\in A[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{i-1}] for all i≥2i\geq 2. By induction on ii, we obtain that xi∈A⁡[Fn+1−i,Fn+2−i,…,Fn]x_{i}\in A[F_{n+1-i},F_{n+2-i},\ldots,F_{n}] for each ii, so FF is invertible. ∎

We showed earlier that ff in (3) is a counterexample to theorem 2.1 with n=4n=4. Using some techniques in the above proof, one can show that ff is a counterexample to theorem 2.2 with n=4n=4 as well. For that purpose, take any T∈GL4⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{4}(K) and any weight function ww such that 0<w⁡(x1)≤w⁡(x2)≤w⁡(x3)≤w⁡(x4)0<w(x_{1})\leq w(x_{2})\leq w(x_{3})\leq w(x_{4}).

Since the rows of the Hessian of the cubic part of ff are independent, there exists a jj such that (ℋ​f​(T​x))n​j∉K({\mathcal{H}}f(Tx))_{nj}\notin K. Furthermore, detℋ​f​(T​x)≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}f(Tx)\neq 0 tells us that there exists an i≥3i\geq 3 and a k≥2k\geq 2 such that (ℋ​f​(T​x))i​k≠0({\mathcal{H}}f(Tx))_{ik}\neq 0. From 0<w⁡(x1)≤w⁡(x2)≤w⁡(x3)≤w⁡(x4)0<w(x_{1})\leq w(x_{2})\leq w(x_{3})\leq w(x_{4}), we deduce that n​w​(f⁡(T​x))−2​w​(x1​x2​x3​x4)≥n​w​(f⁡(T​x))−2​w​(xj​xk​xi​xn)≥w⁡((ℋ​f​(T​x))n​j2​(ℋ​f​(T​x))i​k2)>0nw(f(Tx))-2w(x_{1}x_{2}x_{3}x_{4})\geq nw(f(Tx))-2w(x_{j}x_{k}x_{i}x_{n})\geq w\big(({\mathcal{H}}f(Tx))^{2}_{nj}({\mathcal{H}}f(Tx))^{2}_{ik}\big)>0, which contradicts (4).

3 Proofs of theorem 2.2 and example 2.3

Let us start with a simple case of theorem 2.2.

Proof of the case n=2n=2 of theorem 2.2.

If the leading homogeneous part f¯\bar{f} of ff satisfies detℋ​f¯≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}\bar{f}\neq 0, then we can take w⁡(x1)=w⁡(x2)=1w(x_{1})=w(x_{2})=1 and T=I2T=I_{2}, where I2I_{2} is the identity matrix of size 22. So assume that detℋ​f¯=0\det{\mathcal{H}}\bar{f}=0.

From i) of theorem 2.4, it follows that there exists a T∈GL2⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{2}(K) such that f¯​(T​x)∈K​[x1]\bar{f}(Tx)\in K[x_{1}]. Since f¯​(T​x)\bar{f}(Tx) is homogeneous, we see that its only term is x1dx_{1}^{d}, where d=deg⁡f⁡(T​x)d=\deg f(Tx). By (2) on page 2, we deduce from detℋ​f≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}f\neq 0 that detℋ⁡(f⁡(T​x))≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}(f(Tx))\neq 0. Consequently, f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) has a nonlinear term which is divisible by x2x_{2} besides the term x1dx_{1}^{d}.

Take w⁡(x1)=1w(x_{1})=1. If we take w⁡(x2)=1w(x_{2})=1, then the ww-leading part hh of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) will have the term x1dx_{1}^{d} of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx), but if we take w⁡(x2)≥1w(x_{2})\geq 1 large enough, then hh will not have the term x1dx_{1}^{d} any more, because f∉K⁡[x1]f\notin K[x_{1}].

Now take w⁡(x2)≥1w(x_{2})\geq 1 as large as possible, such that hh still has the term x1dx_{1}^{d} of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx). Since hh will lose the term x1dx_{1}^{d} as soon as w⁡(x2)w(x_{2}) increases only a little further, hh must have another term; a term tt of which the weight will get larger than that of x1dx_{1}^{d} as soon as we start increasing w⁡(x2)w(x_{2}) any further.

From w⁡(t)=w⁡(x1d)w(t)=w(x_{1}^{d}) and deg⁡t<d\deg t<d, it follows that x2|tx_{2}\mid t and w⁡(x2)>w⁡(x1)w(x_{2})>w(x_{1}). Since tt is a term of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) for which w⁡(t)w(t) is maximum and f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) has a nonlinear term which is divisible by x2x_{2}, we deduce that tt is not linear and that hh has no linear terms.

It remains to show that detℋ​h≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}h\neq 0. From i) of theorem 2.4, it follows that it suffices to show that hh cannot be expressed as a polynomial in one linear form in x1x_{1} and x2x_{2}. Hence suppose that hh can indeed be expressed as a polynomial in one linear form. Since the leading homogeneous part of hh is a scalar multiple of x1dx_{1}^{d}, we can take x1x_{1} for this linear form. But t∉K⁡[x1]t\notin K[x_{1}]. Contradiction, so detℋ​h≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}h\neq 0 indeed. ∎

The case n=3n=3 of theorem 2.2 is more complicated. Let us first give a situation where we can do similar things as in the proof of the case n=2n=2 of theorem 2.2, to obtain that theorem 2.2 holds in that situation.

Lemma 3.1.

Let n=3n=3 and assume that f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x] satisfies detℋ​f≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}f\neq 0. Let T∈GL3⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{3}(K) and let ww be a weight function for which 0<w⁡(x1)≤w⁡(x2)≤w⁡(x3)0<w(x_{1})\leq w(x_{2})\leq w(x_{3}).

Suppose that the ww-leading part hh of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) is contained in K⁡[x1,x2]K[x_{1},x_{2}], but is not of the form g1​(l3)​x1+g2​(l3)​x2g_{1}(l_{3})x_{1}+g_{2}(l_{3})x_{2} for any linear form l3∈K⁡[x1,x2]l_{3}\in K[x_{1},x_{2}] and any polynomials g1,g2∈K⁡[x1]g_{1},g_{2}\in K[x_{1}].

Then theorem 2.2 holds for ff. More precisely, we only need to adjust w⁡(x3)w(x_{3}) by increasing it a certain amount in order to get TT and ww as in theorem 2.2 for this particular ff.

Proof.

Take w′​(x1)=w⁡(x1)w^{\prime}(x_{1})=w(x_{1}) and w′​(x2)=w⁡(x2)w^{\prime}(x_{2})=w(x_{2}). By (2) on page 2, we deduce from detℋ​f≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}f\neq 0 that detℋ⁡(f⁡(T​x))≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}(f(Tx))\neq 0. Hence f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) has a nonlinear term which is divisible by x3x_{3}. If we take w′​(x3)=w⁡(x3)w^{\prime}(x_{3})=w(x_{3}), then the w′w^{\prime}-leading part h′h^{\prime} of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) will be just h∈K⁡[x1,x2]h\in K[x_{1},x_{2}]. But if we take w′​(x3)w^{\prime}(x_{3}) large enough, then h′h^{\prime} will not have any term of h∈K⁡[x1,x2]h\in K[x_{1},x_{2}], because the value of w′w^{\prime} at any term which is divisible by x3x_{3} will be larger than w′​(h)w^{\prime}(h).

Now take w′​(x3)≥w⁡(x3)w^{\prime}(x_{3})\geq w(x_{3}) as large as possible, such that h′h^{\prime} still shares a term with hh. From w′​(x1)=w⁡(x1)w^{\prime}(x_{1})=w(x_{1}), w′​(x2)=w⁡(x2)w^{\prime}(x_{2})=w(x_{2}), and h∈K⁡[x1,x2]h\in K[x_{1},x_{2}], we deduce that all terms of hh still have the same weight. Hence h′h^{\prime} contains all terms of hh (with the same coefficients) and w′​(h′)=w⁡(h)w^{\prime}(h^{\prime})=w(h). Furthermore, w′​(t)=w​(t)w^{\prime}(t)=w(t) for any term tt of h′h^{\prime} which is not divisible by x3x_{3}. Hence any such tt is also a term of hh because of w′​(h′)=w⁡(h)w^{\prime}(h^{\prime})=w(h). So x3|h′−hx_{3}\mid h^{\prime}-h.

Since h′h^{\prime} will lose the terms of hh as soon as w′​(x3)w^{\prime}(x_{3}) increases only a little further, h′h^{\prime} must have a term that hh does not have: a term t′t^{\prime} such that w′​(t′)w^{\prime}(t^{\prime}) will get larger than w′​(h′)w^{\prime}(h^{\prime}) as soon as we start increasing w′​(x3)w^{\prime}(x_{3}) any further. Just like for any other term of h′−hh^{\prime}-h, we have x3|t′x_{3}\mid t^{\prime}. Since t′t^{\prime} is a term of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) for which w′​(t′)w^{\prime}(t^{\prime}) is maximum and f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) has a nonlinear term which is divisible by x3x_{3}, we deduce that t′t^{\prime} is not linear and that h′h^{\prime} has no linear terms. Furthermore, we can deduce from the existence of t′t^{\prime} that w′≠ww^{\prime}\neq w, so w′​(x3)>w⁡(x3)w^{\prime}(x_{3})>w(x_{3}).

So it remains to show that detℋ​h′≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}h^{\prime}\neq 0. From ii) of theorem 2.4, it follows that it suffices to show that the following cases do not occur.

  • •

    h′h^{\prime} is of the form g1​(l1)​x1+g2​(l1)​x2+g3​(l1)​x3g_{1}(l_{1})x_{1}+g_{2}(l_{1})x_{2}+g_{3}(l_{1})x_{3} for some linear form l1∈K⁡[x]l_{1}\in K[x] and some polynomials g1,g2,g3∈K⁡[x1]g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}\in K[x_{1}].
    Since h′h^{\prime} contains every term of h∈K⁡[x1,x2]h\in K[x_{1},x_{2}] and x3|h′−hx_{3}\mid h^{\prime}-h, we deduce that h′|x3=0=hh^{\prime}|_{x_{3}=0}=h. Hence h=g1​(l3)​x1+g2​(l3)​x2h=g_{1}(l_{3})x_{1}+g_{2}(l_{3})x_{2} for some linear form l3∈K⁡[x1,x2]l_{3}\in K[x_{1},x_{2}]. But we assumed that hh does not have this form.

  • •

    h′∈K⁡[l1,l2]h^{\prime}\in K[l_{1},l_{2}] for certain linear forms l1,l2∈K⁡[x]l_{1},l_{2}\in K[x] and w⁡(x1)=w⁡(x2)w(x_{1})=w(x_{2}).
    Since w⁡(x1)=w⁡(x2)≤w⁡(x3)w(x_{1})=w(x_{2})\leq w(x_{3}) and h∈K⁡[x1,x2]h\in K[x_{1},x_{2}], we see that hh is the leading homogeneous part of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx). As h′h^{\prime} contains all terms of hh, hh is also the leading homogeneous part of h′h^{\prime}, and just like for h′h^{\prime}, we have h∈K⁡[l1,l2]h\in K[l_{1},l_{2}]. There exists a linear combination of l1l_{1} and l2l_{2} which does not have x3x_{3} as a term, so we may assume that l1∈K⁡[x1,x2]l_{1}\in K[x_{1},x_{2}]. Since hh is not of the form g1​(l3)​x1+g2​(l3)​x2g_{1}(l_{3})x_{1}+g_{2}(l_{3})x_{2} for any linear form l3∈K⁡[x1,x2]l_{3}\in K[x_{1},x_{2}] and any polynomials g1,g2∈K⁡[x1]g_{1},g_{2}\in K[x_{1}], we can deduce that l2∈K⁡[x1,x2]l_{2}\in K[x_{1},x_{2}] as well. This contradicts x3|t′x_{3}\mid t^{\prime}.

  • •

    h′∈K⁡[l1,l2]h^{\prime}\in K[l_{1},l_{2}] for certain linear forms l1,l2∈K⁡[x]l_{1},l_{2}\in K[x] and w⁡(x1)<w⁡(x2)w(x_{1})<w(x_{2}).
    We first show that h∉K⁡[x1]h\notin K[x_{1}] and that the leading homogeneous part h¯′\bar{h}^{\prime} of h′h^{\prime} is divisible by x1x_{1}. Since hh is not of the form g1​(l3)​x1+g2​(l3)​x2g_{1}(l_{3})x_{1}+g_{2}(l_{3})x_{2} for any linear form l3∈K⁡[x1,x2]l_{3}\in K[x_{1},x_{2}], we see that h∉K⁡[x1]h\notin K[x_{1}] indeed and that h∉K⁡[x2]h\notin K[x_{2}]. So h∈K⁡[x1,x2]h\in K[x_{1},x_{2}] has a term t∈K⁡[x1,x2]t\in K[x_{1},x_{2}] which is divisible by x1x_{1}. From w′​(x1)=w⁡(x1)w^{\prime}(x_{1})=w(x_{1}), w′​(x2)=w⁡(x2)w^{\prime}(x_{2})=w(x_{2}) and w′​(x3)>w⁡(x3)w^{\prime}(x_{3})>w(x_{3}), it follows that w′​(x1)<w′​(x2)<w′​(x3)w^{\prime}(x_{1})<w^{\prime}(x_{2})<w^{\prime}(x_{3}). Hence for every term u∈K⁡[x2,x3]u\in K[x_{2},x_{3}] with the same degree as tt, we have w′​(u)>w′​(t)w^{\prime}(u)>w^{\prime}(t).     Since x1|h¯′x_{1}\mid\bar{h}^{\prime}, it follows from lemma 3.2 below that h′∈K⁡[x1,l3]h^{\prime}\in K[x_{1},l_{3}] for some linear form l3∈K⁡[x2,x3]l_{3}\in K[x_{2},x_{3}]. From h′|x3=0=h∉K⁡[x1]h^{\prime}|_{x_{3}=0}=h\notin K[x_{1}], we deduce that h′∉K⁡[x1,x3]h^{\prime}\notin K[x_{1},x_{3}]. So l3l_{3} has a term which is divisible by x2x_{2}. l3l_{3} has a term which is divisible by x3x_{3} as well, because x3|t′x_{3}\mid t^{\prime}. As terms of the expansion of x1s​l3rx_{1}^{s}l_{3}^{r}, x1s​x2rx_{1}^{s}x_{2}^{r} and x1s​x3rx_{1}^{s}x_{3}^{r} are both terms of h′h^{\prime} for some s≥0s\geq 0 and some r≥1r\geq 1, because h′∉K⁡[x1]h^{\prime}\notin K[x_{1}]. This contradicts w′​(x2)<w′​(x3)w^{\prime}(x_{2})<w^{\prime}(x_{3}). ∎

Lemma 3.2.

Suppose that h∈K⁡[l1,l2]h\in K[l_{1},l_{2}] for linear forms l1,l2∈K⁡[x]l_{1},l_{2}\in K[x]. If the leading homogeneous part of hh is divisible by x1x_{1}, then h∈K⁡[x1,l3]h\in K[x_{1},l_{3}] for some linear form l3∈K⁡[x2,x3]l_{3}\in K[x_{2},x_{3}].

Proof.

The leading homogeneous part h¯\bar{h} of hh is contained in k⁡[l1,l2]k[l_{1},l_{2}] as well. Take p∈K⁡[x1,x2]p\in K[x_{1},x_{2}] such that h¯=p⁡(l1,l2)\bar{h}=p(l_{1},l_{2}), and let l3=l1|x1=0l_{3}=l_{1}|_{x_{1}=0} and l4=l2|x1=0l_{4}=l_{2}|_{x_{1}=0}. From x1|h¯=p⁡(l1,l2)x_{1}\mid\bar{h}=p(l_{1},l_{2}), we can deduce that p⁡(l3,l4)=0p(l_{3},l_{4})=0. So l3l_{3} and l4l_{4} are algebraically dependent over KK. Since l3l_{3} and l4l_{4} are linear, they are even linearly dependent over KK. So h∈K⁡[x1,l3]h\in K[x_{1},l_{3}] if l3≠0l_{3}\neq 0 and h∈K⁡[x1,l4]h\in K[x_{1},l_{4}] if l3=0l_{3}=0. ∎

Having lemma 3.1, the strategy will be to reduce to lemma 3.1, under the assumption that theorem 2.2 does not hold, to obtain a contradiction. To do that, we use lemma 3.3 below, after which we prove the case n=3n=3 of theorem 2.2 under the assumption that lemma 3.3 is satisfied. Finally, we will prove lemma 3.3.

Lemma 3.3.

Let n=3n=3 and assume that f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x] satisfies detℋ​f≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}f\neq 0. Suppose that the leading homogeneous part of f⁡(T​x)f(Tx) is of the form x1d−1​l4x_{1}^{d-1}l_{4} for some T∈GL3⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{3}(K) and some linear form l4∈K⁡[x]l_{4}\in K[x].

Then there exist a T∗∈GLn⁡(K)T^{*}\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K) and a weight function ww, such that 0<w⁡(x1)<w⁡(x2)=w⁡(x3)0<w(x_{1})<w(x_{2})=w(x_{3}) and such that the following holds for the ww-leading part h∗h^{*} of f⁡(T∗​x)f(T^{*}x).

  1. a)

    h∗h^{*} is not of the form g1​(l3)​x1+g2​(l3)​x2+g3​(l3)​x3g_{1}(l_{3})x_{1}+g_{2}(l_{3})x_{2}+g_{3}(l_{3})x_{3} for any linear form l3∈K⁡[x]l_{3}\in K[x] and any polynomials g1,g2,g3∈K⁡[x1]g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}\in K[x_{1}].

  2. b)

    detℋ​h∗≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}h^{*}\neq 0 or h∗∈K⁡[x1,x2]h^{*}\in K[x_{1},x_{2}].

Proof of the case n=3n=3 of theorem 2.2.

If the leading homogeneous part f¯\bar{f} of ff satisfies detℋ​f¯≠0\det{\mathcal{H}}\bar{f}\neq 0, then we can take w⁡(x1)=w⁡(x2)=w⁡(x3)=1w(x_{1})=w(x_{2})=w(x_{3})=1 and T=I3T=I_{3}, where I3I_{3} is the identity matrix of size 33.

So assume that detℋ​f¯=0\det{\mathcal{H}}\bar{f}=0. On account of ii) of theorem 2.4, f¯∈K⁡[l1,l2]\bar{f}\in K[l_{1},l_{2}] for some linear forms l1,l2∈K⁡[x]l_{1},l_{2}\in K[x]. We can choose l1l_{1} and l2l_{2} independent of each other, and such that l1l_{1} divides f¯\bar{f} at least as many times as any other linear combination of l1l_{1} and l2l_{2} does.

Take T∈GL3⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{3}(K) such that l1​(T​x)=x1l_{1}(Tx)=x_{1} and l2​(T​x)=x2l_{2}(Tx)=x_{2}. Then the leading homogeneous part f¯′\bar{f}^{\prime} of f′:=f⁡(T​x)f^{\prime}:=f(Tx) is contained in K⁡[x1,x2]K[x_{1},x_{2}], and x1x_{1} divides f′f^{\prime} at least as many times as any other linear form in K⁡[x1,x2]K[x_{1},x_{2}] does. Let d=deg⁡f′d=\deg f^{\prime}. We distinguish two cases.

  • •

    x1d−1∤f¯′x_{1}^{d-1}\nmid\bar{f}^{\prime}.

4 Anisotropic polynomials

The last claim of the main theorem, theorem 2.1, is that the quadratic part of ff is so-called isotropic over KK in case 2≤n≤3≤d2\leq n\leq 3\leq d. The opposite of isotropic is anisotropic. Below, the definition of anisotropic is generalized somewhat.

Definition 4.1.

Let KK be a field of characteristic zero and f∈K⁡[x]=K⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]f\in K[x]=K[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}]. We say that ff is anisotropic over KK at λ∈Kn\lambda\in K^{n} if the quadratic part of f⁡(x+λ)f(x+\lambda) is anisotropic over KK, i.e. does not vanish anywhere at Kn∖{0}nK^{n}\setminus\{0\}^{n}, or equivalently, μt​H​μ≠0\mu^{\rm t}H\mu\neq 0 for all μ∈Kn∖{0}n\mu\in K^{n}\setminus\{0\}^{n}, where

H=(ℋ⁡(f|x=x+λ))|x=0=((ℋ​f)|x=x+λ)|x=0=(ℋ​f)|x=λH=\big({\mathcal{H}}(f|_{x=x+\lambda})\big)\big|_{x=0}=\big(({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=x+\lambda}\big)\big|_{x=0}=({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\lambda} (6)

In the following theorem, the cases n≤3n\leq 3 and K=ℝK={\mathbb{R}} are distinguished. The first case follows from our techniques, while the second case follows from the result by Pogorelov in [Pog], which was mentioned in the introduction. Let GOn⁡(K)\operatorname{GO}_{n}(K) denote the group of orthogonal matrices of size n×nn\times n over KK.

Theorem 4.2.

Let KK be a field of characteristic zero and f∈K⁡[x]=K⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]f\in K[x]=K[x_{1},x_{2},\allowbreak\ldots,x_{n}] such that detℋ​f∈K∗\det{\mathcal{H}}f\in K^{*} and ff is anisotropic over KK at λ\lambda for some λ∈Kn\lambda\in K^{n}. If n≤3n\leq 3 or K=ℝK={\mathbb{R}}, then deg⁡f=2\deg f=2.

Proof.

By assumption, the quadratic part of f⁡(x+λ)f(x+\lambda) does not vanish anywhere at Kn∖{0}nK^{n}\setminus\{0\}^{n}. Hence deg⁡f=deg⁡f⁡(x+λ)=2\deg f=\deg f(x+\lambda)=2 on account the last claim of theorem 2.1 in case n≤3n\leq 3. So assume that K=ℝK={\mathbb{R}}.

Take ν∈ℝn∖{0}n\nu\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}\setminus\{0\}^{n} arbitrary. Then there exists a Tν∈GOn⁡(ℝ)T_{\nu}\in\operatorname{GO}_{n}({\mathbb{R}}) such that

Tνt​(ℋ​f)|x=ν​Tν=Tν−1​(ℋ​f)|x=ν​TνT_{\nu}^{\rm t}({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\nu}T_{\nu}=T_{\nu}^{-1}({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\nu}T_{\nu}

is diagonal, see e.g. [Ser, Cor. 3.3.1]. Hence all eigenvalues of (ℋ​f)|x=ν({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\nu}, which are the same as those of Tνt​(ℋ​f)|x=ν​TνT_{\nu}^{\rm t}({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\nu}T_{\nu}, are real. Suppose that the eigenvalues of (ℋ​f)|x=λ({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\lambda} do not have all the same sign. Then Tλt​(ℋ​f)|x=λ​TλT_{\lambda}^{\rm t}({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\lambda}T_{\lambda} is a diagonal matrix with both positive and negative entries, and we can find a μ∈ℝn∖{0}n\mu\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}\setminus\{0\}^{n} such that μt​Tλt​(ℋ​f)|x=λ​Tλ​μ=0\mu^{\rm t}T_{\lambda}^{\rm t}({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\lambda}T_{\lambda}\mu=0. This contradicts that μt​(ℋ​f)|x=λ​μ≠0\mu^{\rm t}({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\lambda}\mu\neq 0 for all μ∈Rn∖{0}n\mu\in R^{n}\setminus\{0\}^{n}, which is satisfied by assumption because of (6). Hence all eigenvalues of (ℋ​f)|x=λ({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\lambda} have the same sign. By replacing ff by −f-f when necessary, we may assume that all eigenvalues of (ℋ​f)|x=λ({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\lambda} are positive.

From detℋ​f∈ℝ∗\det{\mathcal{H}}f\in{\mathbb{R}}^{*}, it follows that all eigenvalues of (ℋ​f)|x=ν({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\nu} are positive, because of the continuity of eigenvalues, see e.g. [Ser, Th. 3.1.2]. Hence Tνt​(ℋ​f)|x=ν​TνT_{\nu}^{\rm t}({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\nu}T_{\nu} is a diagonal matrix without negative entries, so Tνt​(ℋ​f)|x=ν​TνT_{\nu}^{\rm t}({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\nu}T_{\nu} is positive definite. Consequently, (ℋ​f)|x=ν({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\nu} is positive definite as well. Since the main result of [Pog] tells us that deg⁡f=2\deg f=2 in case detℋ​f∈ℝ∗\det{\mathcal{H}}f\in{\mathbb{R}}^{*} and (ℋ​f)|x=ν({\mathcal{H}}f)|_{x=\nu} is positive definite for all ν∈ℝn\nu\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, the proof is complete. ∎

Corollary 4.3.

The Jacobian conjecture holds for gradient maps over the reals whose linear part is the identity map. More precisely, the corresponding Keller maps are translations.

Proof.

Take K=ℝK={\mathbb{R}} and λ=0\lambda=0 in theorem 4.2, and notice that the quadratic part of ff is 12​(x12+x22+⋯+xn2)\frac{1}{2}(x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+\cdots+x_{n}^{2}) in case the linear part of ∇f\nabla f is the identity map. ∎

A problem for which we do not know the answer, is the following.

Does theorem 4.2 also hold for all fields KK when n>3n>3.

Similarly, 2−i2-{\mathrm{i}} divides both c1c_{1} and c2c_{2}. So 5|c15\mid c_{1} and 5|c25\mid c_{2}, and we have

c32+2​c42+5​(c15)2+15​(c25)2=0c_{3}^{2}+2c_{4}^{2}+5\left(\frac{c_{1}}{5}\right)^{2}+15\left(\frac{c_{2}}{5}\right)^{2}=0

which gives 5|c35\mid c_{3} and 5|c45\mid c_{4} in a similar manner as c12+3​c22+5​c32+10​c42=0c_{1}^{2}+3c_{2}^{2}+5c_{3}^{2}+10c_{4}^{2}=0 gave 5|c15\mid c_{1} and 5|c25\mid c_{2}. This contradicts gcd⁡{c1,c2,c3,c4}=1\gcd\{c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4}\}=1. ∎
